Judge people on what they can do, coach people on what they can do, help them take their strengths and use them as opposed to over focus on their weaknesses and just hand wringing about the one fucking thing they don't know how to do. Because look, everybody's uneven.
turns.zh: 亚当或许是我们做过的最具争议性的投资之一。我们因为资助他而被指责各种罪名——从愚蠢到性别歧视，再到种族主义等等。而我认为，这最终会成为我们做过的最明智的投资之一。他在那里做得非常出色。作为一家公司，我们奉行一个重要的原则，我认为这在业界并不常见，但我希望其他人也能效仿，那就是：不要根据一个人经历过的最糟糕的事情来评判他们。我们都曾遭遇过不幸，也都做过错误的决定。大多数人不会因此拍成迷你剧。（00:52:35）所以评判一个人时，要看他们的优点，而非过错，因为优点才能展现他们的才华。回顾亚当的成就，实在令人惊叹。众人皆知WeWork。说出一个比WeWork更重要的商业地产品牌？找不到。这样的成就实属不易。其间有诸多成功之处和正确决策。（00:53:10）而若要剖析失败根源，大多源于经验不足及身边无人直言相告。当然，他当时或许也不善于听取真言。但就此抛弃一个人——顺便说一句，全世界都因为我们没有抛弃他、选择信任他而对我们大加指责——这实在是个大错。我要称赞马克，因为是他最先联系亚当，问道："亚当，你在做什么？"因为我们观察了你在WeWork的表现，觉得相当出色。（00:53:54）我认为这或许是关键所在。阿尔·戴维斯曾说："要教导球员他们能做什么。"我深以为然。要以他们的能力为准则加以评判，帮助他们发挥优势，而非过度纠结于他们不会的某件事。毕竟，人无完人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What you're describing, essentially, this is the job of an investor, is to find an underappreciated asset and invest or before something people don't see.
turns.zh: 你所描述的，本质上就是投资者的职责——在人们尚未发现价值时，寻找被低估的资产并进行投资。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Venture capital is really about investing in people. You have ideas as an investor, but what you really are ultimately betting on is the entrepreneur and the entrepreneur's idea because the initial idea isn't where they end up usually. It changes a lot with everybody we invest in. So you kind of have to make the judgment on the person. And how you do that is really, really important. And one of the things we emphasize inside the firm is, look, we're investing in strength, not lack of weakness. I want to know how good, are they world-class? Do they have a world-class strength? And can that beat anybody? And look, everybody's flawed. And so let's help them deal with the flaws and surround them with people who can handle that and put the right person on the board who can talk to them. (00:55:43): You know Mark's on the board, I go to all his board meetings because I'm the one who's good at killing a guy who's that confident when he's like, "Okay, that's not your best idea." That's good role for me. But that's how you deal with that. You don't throw them away and go, "Oh, okay, we don't want to be called names. So we're not going to invest in Adam Neumann after we built WeWork. That's crazy.
turns.zh: 风险投资实际上就是对人的投资。作为投资者，你可能有自己的想法，但最终你押注的其实是创业者及其创意，因为最初的构想往往和最终的成果大相径庭。我们投资的每个项目，其初始构想都会随时间发生巨大变化。因此，你必须对创业者本人进行评估，而评估的关键在于——你要看他们是否具备世界级的水准，他们的核心优势能否击败任何竞争对手。当然，每个人都有缺点，我们要帮助他们克服这些缺点，为他们配备能应对挑战的团队，并在董事会中安排能与他们有效沟通的人选。（00:55:43）你知道马克（Mark）在董事会里，我会参加他所有的董事会会议，因为我擅长对那些自信满满的人说“好吧，这不是你最好的主意”。这正是我该发挥作用的地方。但关键在于，不能轻易放弃他们。不能因为怕得罪人，就在投资完WeWork后放弃亚当·诺伊曼（Adam Neumann）——那太疯狂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's also why you guys invested in Cluely, I imagine similar.
turns.zh: 这也是你们投资Cluely的原因吧，我想两者应该很相似。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, no, that's right. I mean, look, if you look at what those guys did, that was some high level marketing genius too, and that's really something. Plus the product is awesome.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我是说，看看那些人的表现，那也是高超的营销智慧，这确实了不起。再加上产品本身也很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to bring us back to AI. Something that a lot of people are talking about right now while we're recording this is this potential huge bubble we're in with AI. Sam Altman said, "We're in a big bubble," which is, that's saying a lot. I'm curious just how you that it-
turns.zh: 接下来我们再聊聊人工智能。录制这期节目时，很多人都在讨论人工智能可能面临的巨大泡沫。山姆·奥特曼（Sam Altman）说“我们正处在一个大泡沫中”，这话很有分量。我很好奇你们对此有何看法——

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: What is it saying? First of all, I should qualify this by saying I am an investor and Sam's a CEO. So CEOs have to have much more purpose when they talk. Investors just have to be entertained. So you got to give Sam credit for what is it in his interest to say it? Well, if it's a bubble, then the one thing you should invest in is him and not all these guys chasing after him. (00:57:09): I would say that's very smart. And then the other thing that's smart about it is there's nothing that you can say to the press that will make them love you more than saying, "All investors and entrepreneurs chasing this are idiots." They love them. The press are generally haters, and so it's just red meat for the haters, which was also super clever. So I think whether even he believes that or not, that was a super smart thing to say. So I'll just put it there. Whereas what I'm going to say won't be as smart, but it will... (00:57:45): I don't really have an ax to grind here. I mean, I could have an ax to grind and say, "Okay, let's get all the other investors out." I'll say, "It's a massive bubble." But what I would say about that is, so the first thing, the one thing about bubbles is anytime everybody thinks it's a bubble, it's not a bubble because in order for it to bubble, you need capitulation. In that you need everybody to believe it's not a bubble, because then the prices really go out of control. But as long as there's people who think it's a bubble, then it's hard for that to happen. And it's funny, I had this debate in The Economist, I think with Steve Blank in like 2011 or '12 when everybody thought it was a tech bubble, if you can imagine that, which it absolutely was not. But because there were 1,400 articles saying that we were in a tech bubble, and I mean where prices were then compared to where they are now. (00:58:52): But I knew because everybody was saying it was a bubble, it wasn't a bubble. I knew that. The prices were higher, but the reason the prices were higher was we're getting to a global market. AI prices are higher than prior prices, but if you look at the revenue growth and numbers, we had not seen anything like it. Sam's product worked so amazingly, we'd never seen that before. Not even Google, not anybody. And so that's real. (00:59:23): And we have companies that went from zero to 800 million in a year and that kind of thing. I would say there's a basis for the prices going up, first of all. I think the thing that's right about what Sam is saying is the landscape is early, really early. The technology is very immature. As amazingly as it works, there's a long way to go to improve it. So it's very possible when you have that much technological change, that the positions that these companies have achieved with their high revenue isn't sustainable, and that there'll be a competitive change that either lowers prices or a new number one emerges or that kind of thing. (01:00:18): Yeah, that's possible. But I wouldn't characterize that as being a financial bubble in that if you go back to the great dot-com bubble that everybody is always waiting for it to happen again, which I was CEO during. The thing that happened there was very different, which is it was the internet and every smart investor knew that the internet was a big deal. How could you not fucking know that the internet was, of course it's a big deal. But if you go back to 1996, at Netscape, we had 90% browser share and we had 50 million users. So there were 55 million people on the internet in total, and half of those were on dial-up. (01:01:03): And then to build a product like Evite, the greeting card company, had 300 engineers. That's how hard it was to build this stuff. And so the math didn't work, and the math didn't work on any of those ideas, but the investors kept pouring money in. And then eventually everybody went bankrupt because there was no revenue coming in. And when they figured that out, then nobody would invest in anything. And of course then everybody realized, well, the internet was actually real and Paul Krugman didn't know what he's talking about, and like it was going to be a big thing. And then Facebook and Google and all these things emerged. (01:01:44): But the thing that made it a bubble was the unit economics didn't work, the businesses didn't work. These businesses are all working, and they're being priced appropriately for how they're growing. So that's not in effect. The thing that you could say is, "They're not going to keep growing like that," and so forth. And I'm not sure about that. The products, like I said, are working so much better than any technology product that we've ever built has worked. It's just mind-blowing how good this stuff is. And so, I don't know, if I had to bet, I would bet not a bubble. I think there'll be some dislocation. I think always in venture capital, if you've got a run like this, then the great company and the crap company both get funded. But that's just venture capital. That's not a bubble.
turns.zh:
它在说什么？首先，我得说明一下，我是一名投资者，而山姆是首席执行官。所以首席执行官在发言时必须更有针对性，而投资者只需要被逗乐。所以你得承认，山姆说那些话是为了自己的利益。（00:57:09）：我觉得这很聪明。另一个聪明之处在于，你对媒体说什么都比不上说‘所有追逐这件事的投资者和创业者都是白痴’更能赢得他们的喜爱。他们本来就对媒体心怀不满，所以这对那些喷子来说就是红肉般的诱饵，这也太聪明了。所以我觉得无论他是否真心这么认为，这番言论都极其高明。所以我就说到这儿。而我要说的可能没那么高明，但至少……（00:57:45）：我在这儿其实没什么私心。我本可以发火说‘好吧，把其他投资者都赶走’，然后说‘这就是个巨大的泡沫’。但我想说的是，关于泡沫的第一条原则是，当所有人都认为这是泡沫时，它就不是泡沫了。因为要形成泡沫，前提是所有人都认为这不是泡沫，这样价格才会失控。但只要还有人认为这是泡沫，泡沫就很难形成。这很有趣，我在《经济学人》上和史蒂夫·布兰克辩论过这个问题，2011或2012年左右，当时所有人都认为是科技泡沫，如果你能想象得到，那根本就不是泡沫。但因为有1400篇文章说我们处在科技泡沫中，而当时的价格和现在相比简直天差地别。（00:58:52）：但我知道因为所有人都说这是泡沫，所以它就不是泡沫。我知道这一点。价格高是正常的，因为我们正在走向全球市场。人工智能的价格比以前高，但如果你看看收入增长和数据，我们从未见过如此规模。山姆的产品效果惊人，我们以前从未见过这种情况。即使是谷歌，也没人能做到。这是真实的。（00:59:23）：而且我们有公司在一年内从零做到8亿美元，诸如此类。我要说的是，首先价格上涨是有基础的。我认为山姆说法的正确之处在于，这个领域还很早期，非常早期。技术还很不成熟。尽管它运行得令人惊叹，但要改进还有很长的路要走。所以很可能当你有如此多的技术变革时，这些公司凭借高收入获得的地位是不可持续的，竞争环境会发生变化，要么降低价格，要么出现新的领头羊之类的。（01:00:18）：是的，这很有可能。但我不会把这归类为金融泡沫。回想起大家一直期待重演的互联网泡沫，我当时就是首席执行官。当时的情况截然不同，那是互联网，每个明智的投资者都知道互联网是个大事。怎么可能他妈的不知道互联网是个大事？但如果回到1996年，网景公司，我们占有90%的浏览器市场份额，有5000万用户。当时互联网总共有5500万用户，其中一半还在用拨号上网。（01:01:03）：然后再建立一个
像电子请帖公司Evite这样的产品，曾有300名工程师参与开发。可见构建这类服务的难度之大。然而这些创意项目最终都未能成功，投资者持续注资却始终不见收益，最终所有参与者都因缺乏营收而破产。人们意识到互联网确实是实实在在的存在，保罗·克鲁格曼当时的预言实在不靠谱——互联网注定会成为一项伟大事业，随后Facebook、谷歌等巨头应运而生。（01:01:44）但导致泡沫形成的根本原因在于商业模式不行、盈利逻辑失效。如今这些公司业务蒸蒸日上，估值也与其增长潜力相符。因此泡沫论的说法站不住脚。当然有人会质疑“它们能否持续高速增长”之类的问题，但我对此持怀疑态度。正如我所说，如今的互联网产品远超我们以往打造的任何科技产品——其卓越程度令人惊叹。因此如果要下赌注，我不会押注泡沫论。我认为这里存在结构性调整。风险投资领域向来如此，市场热潮时优质公司和平庸公司都会获得融资，但这不过是风险投资的常态，绝非泡沫。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Four founders starting companies these days. When you look into the future of the AI industry, say in five, 10 years, how do you think things will play out slash where do you think the biggest opportunities remain? Where are you guys looking to invest most?
turns.zh: 如今四位创始人正在创业。展望未来五到十年的AI行业发展，你认为行业会如何演变？最大的机遇又在哪里？你们最倾向于在哪些领域投资？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: In infrastructure. I think that there is obviously a real estate power cooling play. I think that's a little outside of hardcore technology investing that we do. But there's another layer which is take a given open source model, who can run it the cheapest with the lowest latency? And that's going to be extremely valuable, whoever has that. And Google has been historically very good at that and so forth, and Sam is really trying to build that now with Stargate. And so I think that's going to be a very important layer of value. I think that on the foundation model side, you have to be very selective as an investor. So in order to compete in foundational model world, our basic rule of thumb is you have to be able to, without much product progress, raise at least $ 2 billion because that's basically what it's going to cost you to train something that gets you competitive enough to make money. (01:04:08): And there are just very few founders like that. So Ilya is one of those. Mary's one of those, Fei-Fei is one of those, but that's the kind of class of person you need. And there's whatever. There's certainly less than 10 of those in the world. And so that's kind of an important area, but a small area. And then I think the application layer is going to be very, very interesting. And I think that if you look at Sam, he's making most of his money off ChatGPT, almost all his money off ChatGPT now. And Chat GPT, like it or not, it's got a real moat. It's very hard to knock it off. It's perched. (01:04:57): Everybody's taking a shot at it, people, great distribution like Google and Elon and Zuckerberg and everybody. And that thing just keeps going like it is. So I think the applications are both more complex and kind of stickier than people thought they were originally. The thing that people got very wrong is this whole thin wrapper around GPT, that's really wrong. In fact, here's how wrong it is. Back in the '80s, that same phrase was used, but it was thin wrapper around an RDBMS-
turns.zh: 在基础设施领域。我认为显然存在房地产冷却效应。这有点超出我们硬核技术投资的范畴。但还有另一层挑战——以给定的开源模型为例，谁能以最低成本和最低延迟运行它？谁能做到这一点，将极具价值。谷歌在这方面一直表现出色，而Sam现在正试图通过Stargate项目来实现这一目标。因此，我认为这将成为一个非常重要的价值层面。在基础模型领域，作为投资者必须非常谨慎。为了在基础模型领域竞争，我们的基本原则是，即使没有太多产品进展，也必须能筹集至少20亿美元资金，因为这正是训练出具有足够竞争力并能盈利的模型所需的成本。（01:04:08）：像这样的人才凤毛麟角。Ilya是其中的一个，Mary也是，Fei-Fei也是，但这正是你所需要的级别人才。全球这样的人才肯定不到10个。因此，这是一个重要领域，但规模很小。然后我认为应用层将非常非常有趣。看看Sam，他现在几乎所有收入都来自ChatGPT。无论你喜不喜欢，ChatGPT确实有护城河。很难被超越。它已经站稳了脚跟。（01:04:57）：每个人都在尝试挑战它，比如谷歌、埃隆、扎克伯格等大公司。但它依然势头不减。因此，我认为应用层比人们最初想象的更复杂，也更难以撼动。人们最大的误解是围绕GPT的各种薄壳应用，这实在是大错特错。事实上，错得离谱。回想80年代，就曾出现过类似的现象——但那是围绕RDBMS的薄壳应用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Database.
turns.zh: 数据库。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah. So it meant companies like Salesforce were basically just a thin wrapper. And I think that that's kind of the mistake people made. So we're at this company Cursor, and if you look under the covers in Cursor, they've built 14 different models to really understand how a developer works, a high-end, a real developer. Those models have tons and tons of interactions with how people talk to their friend Cursor about how they should design their programming so forth. And that's real, that's not just a thin layer on a foundation model. And I think there are many, many applications like that. And so I think there's going to be a lot of opportunity at the application layer. There's going to be some opportunity at the foundation model, and of course you can invest in Sam, you can invest in Anthropic and so forth as well. (01:06:43): But there will probably be a very small number of companies at that set, and then a almost unlimited number of companies at the application layer. And then as the technology advances, we'll of course see more things we can body to AI. I mean already autonomous cars are working really well now after a long, long, long, long time. Since I think Sebastian won the challenge in 2006 when he drove the self-driving car across the country. And here we are 20 years later and now they're deployed. So that was a long time. Robots I think is a harder problem than self-driving cars. So we'll see how that goes. But, yeah, there's certainly a lot in that world as well.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，是啊。所以像Salesforce这样的公司基本上就是一个薄薄的封装层。我认为这正是人们犯的错误。所以我们来看看Cursor这家公司，如果你深入了解Cursor的底层技术，他们已经构建了14个不同的模型来真正理解开发者是如何工作的，尤其是高端、真正的开发者。这些模型与用户如何向Cursor的客服团队咨询编程设计等问题有着大量互动。这才是真正的理解，而不是在基础模型上套个薄薄的外皮。我认为有很多这样的应用程序。因此，我认为应用层将会有大量机遇，基础模型层也会有一些机会，当然你也可以投资Sam、Anthropic等公司。（01:06:43）但在基础模型层，可能只有极少数公司能做到，而在应用层，机会则几乎无限。随着技术进步，我们当然会看到更多可以应用到AI的领域。比如自动驾驶汽车经过漫长的研发后，现在已经运行得很好。自从2006年塞巴斯蒂安驾驶自动驾驶汽车穿越美国后，已经过去了20年，现在它们已经投入实际应用了。这确实是个漫长的过程。我认为机器人比自动驾驶汽车更难解决。让我们拭目以待。不过，确实这个领域也有很多机遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, okay. There's a lot to this answer. No, that was exactly what I was looking for. The Cursor example, it's something that comes up a lot on this podcast, in the application layer specifically. The thought that the way to win in this space and to build a moat is, as you said, "Build your own model slash have proprietary data that you build through people using your product." Thoughts on that?
turns.zh: 哇，好的。这个回答内容很丰富。没错，这正是我想了解的。Cursor这个例子，在这个播客里经常被提及，特别是应用层部分。正如你所说，要在这个领域胜出并建立护城河的方法，就是“构建自己的模型，或者拥有通过用户使用产品而积累的专有数据”。对此你有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I think that ends up just being what's required. So it turns out that the universe is long-tailed, is fat-tailed, and humans are very fat-tailed in terms of human behavior, human conversation and so forth. So to get to the real meaning of it and to get to the kind of essence of the problem, in any domain turns out to be, I think, more complex than we thought. And so the early things and people were running around saying, "Okay, there's going to be one big brain to rule them all on these kinds of things." That's kind of not played out yet. (01:08:41): And in fact, if you look underneath the covers, you have LLMs, which have generalized pretty in fascinating ways, but they've kind of also asymptoted in that we have run out of data for the most part. And so if you look at the GPT-5 LLM compared to the GPT-4.1 and how much more it costs to train and so forth, it's definitely not going linear anymore. (01:09:12): On the other hand, the reinforcement learning side has been linear, but it doesn't generalize. So if you build a great programming model, it may be an idiot at math. And so that I think is just very different than what people would've said three years ago. And I think that there's not something that's both scaling and generalizing yet, and maybe we'll get there, but that certainly opens the door to something that's more user-friendly, that's more effective in any number of domains than just the basic foundation model infrastructure. Now those models are incredibly important, and I think OpenAI is probably 80% of the revenue in AI are something like that now. It's massive, and so that foundation model is really, really important. And then the basic consumer app is really, really important. (01:10:12): That just answers whatever the hell you want to know. Those things are very, very real. But I do think particularly, and then if you get into enterprise stuff and then it's no longer internet data, it's their data that becomes very different. Databricks is having a lot of success there because, okay, well, once you're inside a company, guess what? You care about access control. That's hard with an AI world. It gets trained on some stuff. How does it know who has access to that information and who doesn't, and so forth. You have semantic issues. So if you look at an enterprise, find 10 enterprises, they all have a different definition of what a customer means. You would think customer is a basic thing. Well, is it a department at AT&T? Is it AT&T? Is it a person at AT&T? What the hell is the customer? And it turns out to be very, very meaningful, particularly if you're trying to figure out important things like churn and this and that and third. (01:11:19): So that kind of stuff matters. So I would just say the problem space is a lot bigger than you can just attack with a basic foundation model currently. Maybe that will change, and if that changes, then certain prices will have, in retrospect, look way inflated and others will look too low. But that is TBD.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说，我觉得这最终不过是被迫做出的选择。所以结果表明，宇宙是长尾分布，人类行为、人类对话等也都是长尾分布。要想抓住问题的核心本质，在任何领域都比我们想象的要复杂得多。早期的时候，人们四处宣扬：“好吧，总会有一个超级大脑来统治这一切。” 但这种设想至今仍未实现。（01:08:41）：事实上，如果你深入探究，就会发现LLM模型确实进行了令人惊叹的泛化，但它们也遇到了瓶颈——因为数据已经基本枯竭。拿GPT-5和GPT-4.1相比，训练成本的飙升就很能说明问题。（01:09:12）：另一方面，强化学习领域虽然一直保持线性发展，但缺乏泛化能力。比如构建出优秀的编程模型，可能在数学方面却表现得一塌糊涂。我认为这与三年前人们的预期截然不同。目前还没有既能扩展又能泛化的技术，或许未来会实现，但至少当前这为更易用、更高效的应用打开了大门，而这些应用的价值远不止于基础模型基础设施。这些模型至关重要，我认为OpenAI目前80%的AI收入都来自这类模型。规模巨大，所以基础模型确实非常重要。然后，基础消费级应用也同样重要。（01:10:12）：以上就是你想了解的所有东西。这些都是实实在在的问题。但我尤其认为，涉及企业场景时，数据就不再是互联网数据，而是专有数据。这就带来了挑战。比如Databricks在企业领域取得了巨大成功，因为一旦进入企业环境，访问控制就成了核心问题。AI模型在训练过程中会获取大量数据，但谁能访问这些信息，谁不能访问？语义问题同样令人头疼。比如10家不同企业对“客户”的定义可能完全不同。你以为客户是个基本概念，但在AT&T，可能指的是某个部门、整个公司，甚至是某个员工。客户到底是什么？这类问题对理解客户流失等关键指标至关重要。（01:11:19）：所以这些细节至关重要。我想说，当前仅靠基础模型难以攻克的应用场景，未来或许会迎来变革。届时，某些定价或许显得过高，而另一些则显得过低，但一切尚未可知。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a big takeaway from this is that there's still tons of opportunity for founders to start companies building AI products.
turns.zh: 因此，一个重要的启示是，创始人们仍有大量机会创办AI产品公司。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: I think so. Everything that we couldn't solve with software we can solve now, almost. So it's a really big world. And it's funny because we're investors in Waymo, and one of the things when you get into what took so long to make Waymo so safe like they are now, it wasn't the things that everybody reported on the podcast. There wasn't sleet and heavy rain, it was people. It was like the human who was driving 75 in the 25 zone. It was very hard for the AI to anticipate because it was rare but important. And the number of rare, important crazy shit that humans do is very high. And I think that that goes for all of AI. So to make things work really well, you have to understand this very kind of fat tail of human behavior.
turns.zh: 我觉得是这样的。过去我们用软件无法解决的问题，现在几乎都能解决了。所以这是一个广阔的领域。有趣的是，我们是Waymo的投资者。当你深入探究Waymo为何能发展到如今如此安全的水平时，人们关注的焦点往往是那些在播客中被反复提及的挑战——比如雨夹雪、暴雨之类的。但真正关键的因素是人为因素。比如在限速25英里/小时的路段，人们却以75英里/小时的速度行驶。这些看似偶发但至关重要的场景，正是AI难以预测的。而人类这种不可预测的"疯狂行为"实在太多了。我认为这适用于所有人工智能领域。要想让系统真正高效运作，就必须理解人类行为中这种"胖尾分布"般的极端情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along this AI thread, something that is really important to you, clearly something you talk a lot about is the US being successful in AI, in leading the world in AI. Why is this so important? Why is something you spend a lot of time on?
turns.zh: 在关于人工智能的讨论中，你反复强调美国在AI领域的成功，强调美国引领全球AI发展的重要性。为什么这对你如此重要？为什么你要投入大量精力研究这个问题？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: It starts with, I think, my view of the US and its role in the world. My personal view is it's very, very, very important. Not for society to be completely fair because it's not going to be completely fair or completely equal because we've never had one that's been completely equal. But it's important that everybody have a chance at life, and particularly both culturally, but also just you can't advance the world if you can't tap into all of your resources. And so if you kind of take away motivation and these kinds of things, you get into trouble. And if you look at the kind of every country today, and this is by the way, so you want the right amount of decentralized power. You don't want it to be completely concentrated, concentrated power makes it very, very difficult for everybody to have a chance. This is the big lesson of communism over the last hundred years is it turned out right. And we still have politicians selling it this way today, it's like, "Oh, it's power to the people." (01:14:23): No, no, no. It's power to you because you're removing all power from the private sector and installing it into the government, and then you're putting yourself in charge of the government. And so I become extremely powerful. And this is why it didn't matter if it was Mao or Pol Pot or Ceausescu or Stalin, everybody died because when you give anybody that much power, nobody has a chance. There is no incentive, there's no carrot, there's only stick. And so you use that stick, and that's just the nature. It's a system's problem. It's not a person problem. It's not Stalin was evil, Ceausescu is evil. It was that system is evil. And-
turns.zh: 这源于我对美国及其在世界地位的看法。个人认为这非常、非常、非常重要。并非要追求社会的绝对公平——毕竟世界从未实现过完全平等——但确保每个人都有公平的人生机遇至关重要。这不仅关乎文化，更是基于这样一个事实：若无法调动所有资源，世界进步将举步维艰。若剥夺人们的积极性，社会必将陷入困境。观察当今各国现状就会发现，我们需要适度分散权力。权力过度集中会严重限制个体机会。过去百年共产主义的教训告诉我们，过度集权终将导致悲剧。如今仍有政客以"人民赋权"为幌子推销这种体制——（01:14:23）：不不不。这实质上是将权力从私营部门转移至政府，然后由政府掌控权力。这样一来，掌权者就会变得无比强大。毛泽东、波尔布特、齐奥塞斯库、斯大林无不以失败告终，因为权力过度集中必然导致机会消失。没有激励机制，没有奖励机制，只有高压手段。于是人们只能被迫顺从，这就是体制的本质。这不是个人恶魔化的结果——斯大林、齐奥塞斯库固然邪恶，但根本问题在于体制本身。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: It was evil. It was like that system is evil. And that's the saying with fascism. Be it Hitler or Mussolini, it doesn't matter. That level of power is evil. (01:15:11): And the US does the best job. Systematically, it's the best system. It's got all kinds of issues, it's got problems. People always try to defeat it. But one of the things that if you look at the Declaration of Independence or the Constitution, the language is very important. It's, "We hold these truths to be self-evident." (01:15:39): What does that mean? It means it's not my rule, it's not the president's rule, it's God's rule. And so those rules are above the President, and then you work in that context and that distributes the power, because you're under the law, not under the person. We see that now even with Europe, where the leaders are going, "Well, I have a rule. It's you can't say certain things or I'll throw you in jail." And the kind of shield they hide behind as well, we have to keep the kids safe. But if you say something that I don't agree with and the kids hear it, they're not safe. So the kind of transited property of bullshit is going to override. (01:16:29): And so it's really important that we have at least one society. And as flawed as we are, as flawed as the US is, it's still the best. And you can see it by the number of new company creations, the number of new ideas that come out of here and so forth. It's really, really important that the US stays important and powerful in the world. (01:16:51): We know from the last century, if you look at the last century, who were the countries that had economic power, military power, cultural power? They were the ones that industrialized, and the ones that industrialized first and best. And the ones that did became Communists, like Russia, China. They were slow on industrialization and they fell into this very fucking dangerous system. (01:17:19): Looking forward, that's going to happen again, but it's going to be AI. And so it is fundamentally important, not just to America, but to humanity, that America succeed at that. We don't have to be the one winner or this or that, but we do have to be in that tier. (01:17:41): And as I go around the world and travel, I can't tell you, everybody ... and then everybody was getting, by the way, very, very worried about us earlier. And they say, "Look, we need you to succeed. Don't destroy the dollar. Don't fall behind in AI. Don't over-regulate it too early. Don't do these things, please, because we need you to win, because we're all counting on that." (01:18:08): And I think it's the most important work that we do. It's why we're so involved in policy and so forth. I think this is also going to be very, very true with crypto, which ends up being an incredibly important networking technology that complements AI. That work is, I would say, beyond for the money. Although we will end up making a lot of money with the right policies, so I don't want to seem totally philanthropic on this, but it's more important than that. It's certainly more important than us succeeding or anything like that, that the country succeed.
turns.zh: 它太邪恶了。那种体制本身就是邪恶的。这就是法西斯主义的本质。无论是希特勒还是墨索里尼，都无关紧要。那种权力等级本身就是邪恶的。（01:15:11）：而美国做得最出色。在制度层面，它是最完善的体制。它当然有各种问题和缺陷，人们总试图推翻它。但如果你看看《独立宣言》或《宪法》，其中的用词非常重要。例如，“我们认为这些真理是不言自明的”。（01:15:39）：这意味着这不是我的规则，不是总统的规则，而是上帝的规则。因此，这些规则凌驾于总统之上。在这种框架下运作，权力就得到了分配，因为人们受法律约束，而非受个人的支配。如今就连欧洲也是如此，领导人会说：“我有规定，你不能说某些话，否则就把你关进监狱。” 他们还会以保护孩子安全为借口。但如果你说了他们不认同的话，而孩子们又听到了这些言论，那他们就不会安全了。于是这种胡说八道的逻辑就会占上风。（01:16:29）：因此，拥有至少一个运转良好的社会体系至关重要。尽管我们自身存在诸多缺陷，尽管美国也并非完美无缺，但它仍然是最出色的国家。从新公司创立的数量、涌现的新思想等数据可见一斑。保持美国在全球的重要性和影响力对我们至关重要。（01:16:51）：从上个世纪的经验来看，那些拥有经济实力、军事实力和文化影响力的国家是哪些？它们都是最先实现工业化并做得最好的国家。而那些后来共产主义化的国家，比如俄罗斯和中国，则在工业化进程中行动迟缓，最终陷入了极其危险的体制。（01:17:19）：展望未来，类似的情况还会重演，但这次将是人工智能。因此，无论对美国还是全人类而言，美国在人工智能领域取得成功都至关重要。我们不必争当头号强国，但我们必须跻身顶级行列。（01:17:41）：我在全球各地旅行时发现，每个人……顺便说一句，早些时候人们对我们都非常担心。他们说：“看，我们需要你们成功。别毁掉美元。别在人工智能领域落后。别过早地过度监管。别做这些事，拜托了，因为我们需要你们赢得胜利，我们都指望着你们呢。”（01:18:08）：我认为这是我们最重要的工作。正因如此，我们如此投入政策制定等事务。我认为这在加密货币领域也会同样适用，加密货币最终将成为与人工智能相辅相成的极其重要的网络技术。我想说，这份工作远不止为了钱。虽然通过正确的政策我们最终会赚很多钱，所以我不想显得过于慈善，但这比那更重要。这比我们个人的成功或其他任何事情都重要，国家的成功才是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of philanthropic and other passions of yours, something that I don't think most people know about you, and I think will give them another insight into how interesting you are, you run an organization called Paid in Full, which is incredibly cool. Talk about what that's about, why this is so important to you.
turns.zh: 说到你的慈善事业和其他兴趣爱好，我想大多数人都不了解你的一面，我觉得这会让他们对你的趣味性有更深的认识。你运营了一个名为“全额支付”（Paid in Full）的组织，真是太酷了。能谈谈这个组织的宗旨，以及它为何对你如此重要吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Our ethos as a firm is kind of what I'd say is something from nothing. This is the greatness of entrepreneurship. You start with nothing and then you make something really important. That is also how Hip-hop started, where you have a bunch of kids who didn't even have instruments, and they created something out of nothing. And the people in that world always talk about that. (01:19:43): And one of the really unfortunate things that happens is, the people who invent the art form, and certainly in the case of Hip-hop, don't get anywhere near the kind of proportional benefit of their invention. And a lot of the guys, people have forgotten about, or are struggling to make ends meet, and so forth. (01:20:06): So what we created was this thing called the Paid in Full Foundation, named after the Rakim, Eric B. song, which I did call Rakim and ask him for permission to use the name, so we didn't just take it. What we do is, we give essentially pensions to the old rappers, that enable them to kind of continue their work. (01:20:28): And then we have a big event go to paidinfullfoundation.org for tickets, which is amazing, where they get the award and they're celebrated by all their peers and so forth. And it's really phenomenal. Some of the awardees have been Rakim, Scarface from the Geto Boys, Roxanne Shante, Grandmaster Caz, Kool Moe Dee. (01:20:56): This year we're honoring George Clinton for being sampled, Kool G Rap and Grand Puba, and also Jalil from Whodini. I can't even describe how high impact it is on these guys. I think Rakim was touring close to 200 nights a year, and he got his award, and came out with his first album in 15 years and is doing amazingly well. All of a sudden everybody's going, "Oh yeah, that's the greatest rapper of all time." They're finally going back and remembering all the things he did. Roxanne Shante, nobody had mentioned her in years and years and years. I think six months after we gave her the award, the Grammys gave her a lifetime achievement award, which is amazing. It's super high impact. It's a great thing. As a Hip-hop fan, I say dream come true. It's my only guilt.
turns.zh: 我们的公司理念可以用一句话概括，那就是"一无所有，却能成就大业"。这就是创业精神的伟大之处。你从零开始，然后创造出非凡的价值。嘻哈音乐的诞生也是如此，当时一群甚至没有乐器的孩子，硬是从无到有地创造出了一种文化。这也是嘻哈界的人们常津津乐道的话题。（01:19:43） 然而令人遗憾的是，开创艺术形式的人——尤其是嘻哈音乐的先驱们——往往得不到与其贡献相匹配的回报。许多开创者要么被遗忘，要么在艰难维生。（01:20:06） 因此，我们创立了"Paid in Full基金会"，这个名字源自Rakim和Eric B.的歌曲。我亲自联系了Rakim并获得授权，并非擅自挪用。我们为资深说唱歌手提供养老金支持，让他们得以继续创作。（01:20:28） 每年我们都会举办盛大的颁奖典礼，入场券可登录paidinfullfoundation.org购买。这场盛会意义非凡，获奖者能获得同行致敬，重新被世人铭记。今年的获奖者包括George Clinton、Kool G Rap和Grand Puba，以及Whodini的Jalil。这些获奖者对行业的影响力之大，令人惊叹。Rakim曾每年巡演近200场，获奖后不仅推出了15年来的首张专辑，还取得了巨大成功。突然间所有人都惊呼："他才是史上最伟大的说唱歌手！"人们终于重新审视他的贡献。Roxanne Shante多年来无人问津，但在我们授予她奖项的六个月后，格莱美授予她终身成就奖，这太不可思议了。这种影响力是巨大的，这真是了不起的事业。作为嘻哈乐迷，我觉得梦想成真了。这是我唯一的遗憾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the origin story of you and Hip-hop? I imagine many people look at you and wouldn't imagine these records behind you, Nas gifted you. You are so deep into the community, just how did this all begin?
turns.zh: 你和嘻哈音乐的缘分是怎样的？我想很多人看到你，根本想象不到你身后有这些唱片，Nas曾把唱片送给你。你深深扎根于这个圈子，一切是如何开始的？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Well, I actually wrote a blog post on it called The Legend of the Blind MC, which I think would be, if you're really interested, it's worth reading. But it is kind of a story of me becoming a rapper, and how that occurred, and how it went, and so forth. (01:22:23): I always say the very short story is, I was in New York at the birth of Hip-hop and when it really became big, '84 through '88. It's just the most exciting thing to see a new art form pop out and the creativity and everything. (01:22:43): Once music becomes mainstream, I would say it's very shaped by business. And in the early days, everybody's just coming out with whatever idea they have and so forth. The early days of rock and roll were like that. The early days of jazz were like that.
turns.zh: 嗯，我其实写过一篇博文，叫《盲人说唱歌手的传奇》，如果大家感兴趣，可以去读一读。但这基本上就是我成为说唱歌手的故事，过程如何，成果如何等等。（01:22:23） 我常说最简短的版本是：我在纽约见证了嘻哈音乐的诞生和它真正火起来的时候，1984到1988年间。这是见证一种新艺术形式诞生、见证创造力和一切的最激动人心的时刻。（01:22:43） 一旦音乐成为主流，我认为它就被商业所左右了。早期，每个人都只是凭着自己的想法创作，顺其自然。摇滚乐的早期就是这样，爵士乐的早期也是如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see now even more why you guys brought on Erik Torenberg. Beyond his many talents, he's also really big into rap himself.
turns.zh: 现在我更明白为什么你们请了Erik Torenberg了。除了他多才多艺，他自己也对说唱乐非常热衷。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yeah, that's a good reminder. I need to make sure he gets to Paid in Full.
turns.zh: 是啊，这是个很好的提醒。我得确保他能去参加Paid in Full活动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ben, this was incredible. Is there anything else that you want to leave listeners with or share before we get to our very exciting, quick lightning round?
turns.zh: 班，这太棒了。在我们进入令人兴奋的快速问答环节之前，你还有什么想留给听众或分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yeah, I would just say, if you're a CEO listening to this, then know that how you feel about yourself is going to end up meaning as much as anything, and take your time on that. Self-evaluation is ... one of my favorite quotes is that when my old manager saw me, as select players know, "From this day on, no credit will be given for predicting rain, only credit for building an ark." (01:24:05): And I think that's more true for CEOs than anybody. You have to build the ark. It doesn't matter if you predict you're going to fail, you've still failed. It gets you nothing. So what you have to do is figure your way out of it and spend all your time on that.
turns.zh: 是的，我只想说，如果你是一位听众CEO，那你要知道，你对自己的看法最终会和其他任何事情一样重要，所以请花时间好好思考这个问题。自我评估……我最喜欢的名言之一是，当我的老经理看到我时（正如选手们都知道的）：“从今天起，再也没有人会因为预测下雨而给你赞誉，只有建造方舟的人才会被认可。”（01:24:05）我认为这对CEO们比对其他人更适用。你必须亲手建造方舟。即使你预测自己会失败，那也依然是失败。这种预测毫无意义。所以你必须想办法走出困境，并把所有时间都投入到这件事上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，现在我们要进入激动人心的快速问答环节了。我有五个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yes, sir.
turns.zh: 是的，先生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people, not including your own books?
turns.zh: 第一个问题：除了你自己的书之外，你最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: So two that I learned a lot from, one is The Weirdest People in the World, which it's a kind of big history book, but through an anthropological kind of cultural lens. It's really fascinating. It explains an awful lot about how society works and how little changes in the rules completely change the culture. (01:25:02): One of the things that he basically endeavors to explain, why did the West get ahead on the rest of the world? It kind of comes down to a weird anomaly with the Catholic Church, where they enforced monogamous marriage. And it turns out that the natural state of humans is polygamy, but the problem with polygamy is, there's no cooperation among men, which is a problem. And as a result, and then everything is secret, so there's no sharing of knowledge, because it's all kept in the family, in what he calls kin-based culture. (01:25:44): It leads to something called kin-based culture. And even recipes won't be shared if you're in a kin-based culture, because it's a secret. So you can't build science, you can't build cities, you can't build big companies. So because the West kind of enforced broad monogamous marriage early, it was able to evolve into all these things. (01:26:07): And he kind of shows why and how. He does these psychological tests today with people from monogamous marriage culture, Western culture, and kin-based culture. And the psychology is completely different. He gives examples like if a person murders another person, is that still murder if that person who did the murder is your brother? And in Western society, yeah, that's a murder. In kin-based culture, it's not a murder. It's just not. (01:26:39): And so that's really different. And so morality is different, everything comes off of that. So it's just a fascinating, fascinating book. So that's one. (01:26:55): Another book that I recommend a lot is Shaka's book, his first book, Writing My Wrongs. He has a new book that I think is better, which is called How to Be Free. It's not quite out, or maybe it's releasing. It's releasing next month, so I recommend it. (01:27:11): What it does is, it goes through how did he work his way out of prison and solitary confinement to his current psychology, and what are the techniques he used? They're very powerful, very powerful ideas. CEOs always asks me, "How do you deal with it? How do you deal with it?" They'll ask in a work-life balance. It's like, "What are you talking about? No work-life balance for CEOs," or particularly entrepreneur CEOs, come on. (01:27:43): But what do you do? Do you meditate? Do you do this or that? But he kind of goes through the things that you really ought to do. That's what I would recommend, if somebody's wondering, how do you deal with all this pressure?

以下是用户提供的英文文本的中文翻译：

我学到很多东西的两本书，一本是《世界上最奇怪的人们》，这是一本大型历史著作，但通过人类学的文化视角来解读。真的很引人入胜。它深刻解释了社会运作机制，以及规则的微小变化如何彻底改变文化。（01:25:02）：他试图解释的一个问题是，西方为何能领先于世界其他地区？这归结于天主教会强制推行一夫一妻制的奇特现象。原来，人类的自然状态是多配偶制，但多配偶制的问题在于男性之间缺乏合作，这是一个顽疾。因此，一切都处于保密状态，知识无法共享，因为信息都被家族内部掌控，他称之为血亲文化。（01:25:44）：这种文化导致了血亲文化的形成。即使在血亲文化中，食谱也不会被分享，因为信息是保密的。因此，科学无法发展，城市无法建设，大型公司也难以兴起。正因为西方早期强制推行广泛的一夫一妻制，它才得以发展出这些成就。（01:26:07）：他通过心理测试展示了原因和机制。他对来自一夫一妻制文化（西方文化）和血亲文化的人进行测试，发现心理差异巨大。例如，如果一个人杀害了另一个人，如果被杀者是自己的兄弟，这还算谋杀吗？在西方社会，这就是谋杀；但在血亲文化中，这不算谋杀。（01:26:39）：这就是巨大的差异。因此，道德观也不同，一切都源于此。这本书真是引人入胜。我强烈推荐第一本《写下我的过错》。他的新书《如何获得自由》更胜一筹，虽然尚未出版，或许下个月就会发布，我强烈推荐。（01:27:11）：这本书讲述了他如何从监狱和单独监禁中走出来，形成如今的心理学观点，分享了哪些技巧？这些理念非常强大，非常有力。CEO们总是问我：“如何应对压力？如何平衡工作与生活？” 这就像在说，“CEO怎么可能平衡工作与生活？” 尤其是创业型CEO，更是天方夜谭。（01:27:43）：但你该怎么做？冥想？采取某种措施？但他详细列出了真正应该做的事。这就是我的建议，如果有人想知道如何应对压力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. Just the whole idea of Shaka being this help for CEOs, someone that killed someone, went to prison, led a prison gang. I just love that, how valuable his lessons-
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这本书了。单单沙卡的经历就令人惊叹——他杀过人，入过狱，还领导过监狱帮派。我特别欣赏他的教诲——

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Prison gangs turn out to be really complicated things to manage. Sorry for getting into this, but the problem with running a prison gang is, you're just dealing with people who all come from broken culture. (01:28:23): So in any organization, like the fundamental thing is trust. And so you're bringing in a bunch of no trust people. And so again, it's kind of like a military organization. It's a gang. If you think about a military operation, if you don't have trust, people don't trust the order, then you're completely dysfunctional. (01:28:46): So how do you build trust from zero is a very interesting problem. And he's a genius at that, by the way. And I learned a lot from talking to him about it. So from a management standpoint, I would just say it's an important kind of boundary case of how you build culture. He is very, very smart at that. Like I said, you have to look at people about their greatness, not the worst thing they ever did.
turns.zh: 监狱帮派的管理实在是件复杂的事。抱歉说到这个话题，但管理监狱帮派的难点在于，你面对的都是来自破碎文化背景的人们。（01:28:23）所以在任何组织中，最基本的要素就是信任。但你面对的都是缺乏信任的人。这就有点像军事组织。帮派也是如此。如果你不信任命令，整个组织就会陷入瘫痪。（01:28:46）所以如何从零开始建立信任，是个非常有趣的问题。顺便说一句，他在这方面堪称天才。和他探讨这个问题让我受益匪浅。从管理角度来看，这其实是如何构建文化的重要边界案例。他在这方面非常高明。正如我所说，评判一个人要看他的伟大之处，而不是他做过的最糟糕的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know it's the lightning round, but can you just share one example of something he did that was like, wow, that's a really good lesson, someone trying to create a good culture that worked for him?
turns.zh: 我知道这是闪电问答环节，但你能否分享一个他做过的例子，比如，哇，这真是个很棒的教训，某人试图营造一个对他有效的良好文化？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yeah. So one of the things that he did that I thought was really smart is ... Well, he did a couple of things. One is just a simple thing. He just made everybody eat lunch together in the gang, just to build rapport, relationship, trust, like it's all one thing. We're all together on that. (01:29:56): And I think particularly in the remote work world and so forth, people really underestimate how powerful just that idea can be. And then another thing he did is, he made morality ... he had very specific things about, you had to be good to your word internally and externally. (01:30:26): So normally a gang, like I said, it's kind of a kin-based culture thing. But it made it much more powerful when he said, "Look, you can't do devious shit outside the gang either." And he had a bunch of examples of that, that I went through in the book. (01:30:50): Like I said, because you're building it from zero, you really have to take a hard line on things that I think people in companies don't even take a hard line on. Is it okay to lie internally? Probably not. Is it okay to lie to a customer? Well, in some organizations it is, but in Shaka's organization, that's as big a penalty as lying internally. These things, I think, end up being really important.
turns.zh: 是的。他做过几件事，我觉得特别明智。其中之一很简单。他让帮派里的每个人一起吃午餐，就为了建立融洽关系、信任感。我们都在同一条船上。（01:29:56）我认为尤其是在远程工作环境中，人们严重低估了这种理念的威力。还有一件事是，他强化了道德规范……他有非常具体的要求，比如内部和外部都要守信。（01:30:26）通常帮派是基于亲属文化的。但他说：“听着，你在帮派外也不能干坏事。”他举了很多例子，我在书中都详细写了。（01:30:50）正如我所说，因为你从零开始建立文化，你必须在一些事情上采取强硬立场，而这些事情很多公司甚至都不敢管。比如内部撒谎可以吗？大概不行。对客户撒谎可以吗？有些组织允许，但在沙卡的组织里，这和内部撒谎一样严重。这些问题最终变得非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to link to this book. This is, What You Do is Who You Are. This is your second book that fewer people know about. And this is one of the stories you tell and just what the lessons are for building-
turns.zh: 我们会链接到这本书。《你做什么，你就是谁》。这是你的第二本书，知情者较少。我在书中讲述了其中一个故事，以及构建文化的经验教训。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yeah. It's kind of the more advanced book. You kind of have to survive to want to care about dealing with the cultural issues. And so the survival book has a bigger audience.
turns.zh: 是的。这本书更具深度。只有在历经风雨后的人才会愿意关注文化问题。所以生存类书籍的受众更广。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. We're going to keep going with Lightning Round. Is there a favorite recent movie or TV show you have really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们继续闪电问答环节。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Well on TV, I really like Slow Horses, which is the show about the MI6 cast-off guys. And then I haven't seen a lot of movies lately, but I watched Sinners. I went to theater for Sinners. Just the cinematography is unbelievable, and the story is really original, and the acting is incredible, and the costumes are amazing. It's just a great, comprehensive piece of work. The craftsmanship on that thing is just a lot beyond what most people making movies are doing these days, so I really enjoyed that.
turns.zh: 嗯，电视方面，我特别喜欢《慢马》这部剧，讲的是军情六处被抛弃的特工们的故事。最近电影看得不多，但我看了《罪人》。我特意去电影院看了这部片子。光是摄影效果就令人惊叹，故事构思独具匠心，演员表演也极其出色，服装设计更是令人赞叹。这真是一部全面出色的作品。影片的制作水准远超当下大多数电影制作者的水平，所以我特别喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I hate scary movies, but I watched it and loved it.
turns.zh: 我讨厌恐怖片，但我看了这部片子，结果还挺喜欢的。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: It wasn't that scary.
turns.zh: 它其实没那么恐怖。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It wasn't that scary, but still, it was zombies popping out of corners. That's not my jam usually. (01:32:35): Is there a product you recently discovered that you really love? It could be a gadget, it could be clothes, could be something else.
turns.zh: 虽然没那么恐怖，但还是有僵尸从角落里跳出来那种场景。这通常不是我的菜。（01:32:35）：你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？可能是小玩意、衣服，或者其他东西。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: I bought a coffee machine called the Technivorm Moccamaster, which is freaking incredible. In fact, a friend of mine saw it and was like, "What is that?" And I just bought it for him too, because it's so awesome. This thing makes coffee that it's just perfect. There's no bitterness. It's completely clean. It's amazing. The only problem with it is, I can't drink coffee that it doesn't make anymore. I don't know if that's a good thing or bad thing, but ...
turns.zh: 我买了一台叫Technivorm Moccamaster的咖啡机，那东西简直太棒了。事实上，我一个朋友看到它后问：“这是什么？” 我还给他也买了一台，因为它太赞了。这台咖啡机做的咖啡堪称完美。没有苦味，口感清爽。太棒了。唯一的问题是，我现在喝不到它做出来的咖啡了。不知道这是好事还是坏事，不过...

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That might come out someday in the AI future.
turns.zh: 说不定未来某天人工智能能解决这个问题。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two more questions. One, is there a life motto that you often come back to, find really useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 再问两个问题。第一个，你有没有一条人生格言，经常回想起来，觉得对工作或生活特别有用？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: The thing that I would say has had the biggest effect on me is something my father said to me years ago, which is, "Life isn't fair." That seems really, really simple, but I think that the thing that defeats people more than any other thing that I've seen, just in life, is the expectation of some fairness. It's just not fair. (01:33:54): There are all kinds of stuff that are going to happen to you, and happen to everybody, that don't happen to other people, that are completely unfair. But it doesn't matter, because that's the way it is. As soon as you get that idea out of your mind, then you can just deal with it, like, oh yeah, of course it's not fair, but what should I do now, which is the real question, not how do I go back and get people to be fair? Nobody's going to be fair. It's not fair. (01:34:25): It's the nature of it. If you think about it for more than five seconds, you'll realize that. It's as an individual, if you want to make the world a better place, whatever, but as an individual, do not expect anything to be fair, it'll only defeat.
turns.zh: 对我影响最大的，是我父亲多年前对我说的一句话：“生活不公平。” 这听起来简单极了，但我发现，在生活中最能打败人的东西，就是对公平的期待。生活本来就不公平。（01:33:54）：总有各种各样的事会发生在你身上，也会发生在每个人身上，而其他人却不会经历，这些事完全不公平。但这没关系，因为生活本来就是这样。一旦你不再纠结于此，你就能坦然面对，心想，哦，对啊，当然不公平，那现在该怎么做，这才是关键问题，而不是如何让别人变得公平。没人会公平。生活本来就不公平。（01:34:25）：这就是它的本质。如果你仔细想五秒钟以上，你就会意识到这一点。作为个体，如果你想让世界变得更美好，那随你便，但作为个体，别指望任何事是公平的，这只会让你挫败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. This comes from Shaka, actually. He gave me so many great suggestions. I hate to save this one for last. So the question is, if you had to build a business curriculum from two Hip-hop albums and one Funk album, what would they be and why?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。这个问题其实来自Shaka。他给了我很多很棒的建议。我不想把这个问题留到最后。所以问题是，如果你要用两张嘻哈专辑和一张放克专辑来构建商业课程，会选哪几张，为什么？

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: I think probably Follow the Leader by Rakim. And the reason is what we had kind of gotten into earlier, which is leadership. When he came out with that song, which was maybe the greatest Hip-hop song ever written, he's telling people to follow him, follow the leader. And just to have the idea that he was the leader of the entire art form, not just his band, it is amazing idea. And then the way he expressed it was incredible. And then he's got other great concepts in there that would give you ... It's hard to listen to that record and not have confidence. (01:36:02): I think from a competitive, purely competitive standpoint, Stillmatic from Nas, that's the one with Get Ur Self a Gun, that's the one with You're da Man. It's like all of the idea of competition is encapsulated in that album, so that would be the other one. (01:36:26): And then Funk, One Nation Under a Groove, for sure. Because it's like, how do you initiate people into a concept or an idea, and how do you infuse them? One Nation Under a Groove is all about joining the nation, and it's so musically interesting and getting people to be part of that. [inaudible 01:36:58] If you asked me tomorrow, I'd probably have three other ones.
turns.zh:
我觉得可能是Rakim的《Follow the Leader》。原因在于我们之前讨论过的领导力话题。当他推出这首歌曲——这或许是史上最伟大的嘻哈歌曲——时，他呼吁人们追随他，追随领袖。单是他自视为整个艺术形式的领袖，而不仅仅是乐队领袖的这个理念，就令人惊叹。而他传达这一理念的方式更是令人赞叹。专辑中还有其他深刻的概念，听完这张专辑，你很难不被赋予信心。

（01:36:02）：从纯粹竞争的角度来看，我会选Nas的《Stillmatic》，那张有《Get Ur Self a Gun》和《You're da Man》的专辑。整张专辑完美诠释了竞争的理念，堪称此类主题的典范。

（01:36:26）：还有《Funk, One Nation Under a Groove》，这张专辑无疑是经典之作。它探讨了如何让人们接纳某种理念，并深深融入其中。《One Nation Under a Groove》致力于凝聚国家力量，音乐性极高，成功将人们带入这场盛会。

[01:36:58不可听清]如果明天再问我，我可能还会再列出三个专辑。

turns.en: Incredible. I'm going to go listen to these. Ben, final question, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我要去听听这些专辑了。本，最后一个问题：听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.en: If you get something that makes you better, please take it. If you need more advice on it, let me know. Look, my job is to help everybody build something great, so if you're an entrepreneur, thank you for that.
turns.zh: 如果你能从中收获成长，请务必吸收。如果需要更多建议，随时告诉我。听着，我的工作就是帮助大家创造伟大的事业，所以如果你是一位创业者，我要感谢你。

turns.en: Also, check out Paid in Full, paidinfullfoundation.org, if you want to learn more about that nonprofit.

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: Yes, definitely, we would love to have you.
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。非常感谢你能来。

turns.en: Amazing. Ben, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。本，非常感谢你的参与。

turns.speaker: Ben Horowitz
turns.en: All right, awesome. Thank you, Lenny.
